_comment: Introductions shown in the hero on each book page, beside the title. Keyed by page slug rather than book name: book_blurbs.json derives its key by slugifying the name it carries, which silently lost Al-Tawḥīd and Muʿjam al-Aḥādīth al-Muʿtabara when that name did not match the catalogue's.
al-kafi: Compiled by Muḥammad b. Yaʿqūb al-Kulaynī (d. 329/941) over roughly twenty years in Rayy and Baghdad, al-Kāfi is the earliest of the Four Books and the most widely cited collection in Twelver Shi'ism. It is built in three parts. The Uṣūl gathers narrations on belief — the standing of reason, the oneness of God, prophethood, and the imamate — and is read as a doctrinal source in its own right. The Furūʿ covers practice across purity, prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, marriage, inheritance, trade and judgement. The Rawḍa, belonging to neither, collects sermons, letters and reports that fit no other heading. Al-Kulaynī worked during the period of the shorter occultation, close enough to the Imams' circles to draw on the written notebooks of their companions directly, and much of what survives of those earlier sources survives because it passed through here. Where later compilers selected, he recorded — which is why the book is large, and why it is argued over.
man-la-yahduruh-al-faqih: The second of the Four Books, written by Shaykh al-Ṣadūq (d. 381/991) for a patron in Balkh who had no scholar nearby to consult, and named after a medical handbook written for the same situation. Its title — 'for one who has no jurist at hand' — states its method. Rather than record everything transmitted, al-Ṣadūq included only what he was prepared to rely on, writing that he offered these reports as proof between himself and God. That editorial stance makes it the most opinionated of the Four Books and the most immediately usable: it is organised as a working legal reference, from purity and prayer through commerce, marriage, inheritance and judgements. Chains are usually shortened or dropped in the text itself, with the full paths collected separately in the mashyakha at the end, so the reader meets the ruling first and the transmission afterwards — an arrangement later scholars have both praised for clarity and scrutinised for what it leaves implicit.
nahj-al-balagha: Sermons, letters and short sayings of Imam ʿAlī, selected by al-Sharīf al-Raḍī (d. 406/1015) — a poet himself — for their eloquence as much as their content. The arrangement follows that purpose: the sermons first, then the correspondence, then several hundred aphorisms. The range is unusually wide, from the metaphysical to the immediately administrative: sermons on creation and the limits of describing God sit near letters appointing governors and auditing their conduct. Among them is the long letter of instruction to Mālik al-Ashtar on governing Egypt, read on its own as a treatise on just rule, and the account of the Battle of Ṣiffīn's aftermath. Because al-Raḍī chose by literary criterion and often kept only the passage that moved him, dropping chains and context, the work has been studied both as a monument of Arabic prose and as a doctrinal source — and its transmission has been debated for as long as it has been read.
al-amali: The 'dictations' of Shaykh al-Ṣadūq: not a compiled reference but a record of teaching sessions, each assembly dated and placed, delivered across Rayy, Nishapur, Baghdad and elsewhere in the late fourth century. The material moves as a lesson moves — a narration on ethics, then one from the life of the Prophet or an Imam, then a point of doctrine, then something on the merits of a companion — rather than being sorted by subject. Several assemblies fall on days of particular significance and take their subject from the occasion, including the sessions on the events of Karbalā. Read straight through, the book shows what a leading scholar of his generation chose to put in front of an audience, in what order, and to whom, which is a different kind of evidence from a systematic collection: it records not only what was transmitted but what was thought worth teaching.
al-khisal: Shaykh al-Ṣadūq's collection arranged entirely by number: traditions that enumerate one thing, then two, then three, ascending through the book to the largest figures. The ordering is a memory device rather than a subject index — it is how material was held before it could be looked up — so a single chapter moves from the three things that ruin a person to the three that save him to the three whose prayers are not refused. The result spans ethics, law, cosmology, history and etiquette, gathered by the shape of the report rather than its topic, which puts unrelated material side by side and makes the book unexpectedly good for browsing. It preserves a great deal found nowhere else, including the long treatise on rights attributed to Imam Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn, and it is among the most frequently quoted of al-Ṣadūq's works for exactly that reason.
kitab-al-ghayba: Shaykh al-Ṭūsī (d. 460/1067) on the occultation of the twelfth Imam, written in Baghdad more than a century after the events it describes and at a moment when the doctrine was under sustained attack. It is not only a collection. Al-Ṭūsī sets out the reports, argues from them, and then answers his opponents directly — that a leader nobody can reach is no leader, that the length of the concealment tells against it, that the accounts contradict one another. He documents the four deputies said to have carried communication during the shorter occultation, the letters attributed to that period and the disputes over who could claim to represent the Imam, including the claimants he rejects. He also collects earlier reports of concealment among previous prophets, arguing the pattern is not new. It remains the principal early Imāmī treatment of the subject, and later discussions largely work from the ground it laid.
thawab-al-a-mal-wa-iqab-al-a-mal: Two complementary works of Shaykh al-Ṣadūq, usually printed and read as one: the rewards promised for particular acts, and the punishments warned of for particular sins. Each entry is short and specific — a prayer said at a certain time, a fast kept, a visit made, a kindness to a parent or a neighbour; and on the other side, a betrayal, a false oath, a withheld right, a severed tie. The pairing is the point: the two halves cover the same ground from opposite directions, so a subject can be read as encouragement and as warning together. Because the entries are concrete and quotable they are among the most cited sources in sermons and devotional writing, which has also drawn criticism — several chains are weak, and al-Ṣadūq's own practice was to transmit what he received in this genre more readily than in law. Read as a map of what the tradition treats as consequential rather than as a legal authority.
uyun-akhbar-al-rida: Shaykh al-Ṣadūq's gathering of everything he could assemble concerning ʿAlī b. Mūsā al-Riḍā, the eighth Imam, composed for the Buyid vizier al-Ṣāḥib b. ʿAbbād. It runs from the Imam's sayings and correspondence to accounts of his journey to Khurāsān, his appointment as heir apparent by the caliph al-Maʾmūn and the politics behind it, the debates he is recorded as holding at court with Christian, Jewish and Zoroastrian scholars, his replies on divine unity and free will, and the circumstances of his death and burial at Ṭūs. It also preserves the report known as the Golden Chain, transmitted through his forefathers to the Prophet. Because it is organised around one figure rather than one subject, it reads as a life as much as a collection — the only book of its kind among al-Ṣadūq's works, and the main source for the period it covers.
ma-ani-al-akhbar: Shaykh al-Ṣadūq on the meanings of the reports: a collection assembled specifically to explain difficult words, obscure phrases and apparently strange statements found elsewhere in hadith. Its method is what makes it unusual — the explanation is itself a narration, so the book is a commentary built entirely out of other transmitted material rather than the compiler's own gloss. A term in one report is clarified by another report in which an Imam is asked what it means. The range runs from single words of old Arabic to whole statements whose surface sense seems to conflict with doctrine, including several that opponents raised as objections. It is consulted when a narration elsewhere is clear in its wording and unclear in its sense, and it is one of the earliest sustained attempts in the tradition to treat interpretation as a transmitted science rather than an individual judgement.
kamil-al-ziyarat: Ibn Qūlawayh (d. 368/978), a teacher of al-Shaykh al-Mufīd, on ziyāra: the visitation of the Prophet and the Imams, and above all of Imam al-Ḥusayn at Karbalā. Across just over a hundred chapters it gathers the merit attached to the visit, the rites and words prescribed for it, the standing of the earth of Karbalā, the weeping of creation for al-Ḥusayn, and accounts of those who made the journey when doing so was dangerous. It is the earliest surviving work devoted to the subject and the source most later ziyāra texts draw on. The book is cited nearly as often for its preface as its contents: there the author states that he included only what reached him through reliable transmitters among the companions. Whether that amounts to authenticating every chain in the book, or only the sources he names, has been argued by scholars from his own century to the present, and the question still divides them.
al-tawhid: Shaykh al-Ṣadūq on divine unity, and the most sustained argument among his works. It gathers narrations on God's oneness, His names and attributes, His knowledge, will and justice, and the rejection of any likeness between God and what He created. It was written against positions al-Ṣadūq regarded as errors on two fronts at once: anthropomorphism, which read reports of God's hand or face literally, and a determinism that made human action meaningless and divine justice empty. The arrangement follows that polemic rather than a neutral order, and several chapters carry recorded debates — with dualists, with materialists, with Muslim opponents — in which the argument is carried out rather than asserted. It is the standard early Imāmī statement on the subject, and later theological writing in the tradition tends to begin from the material collected here.
mu-jam-al-ahadith-al-mu-tabara: A modern compilation that admits only narrations meeting its compiler's stated criteria for reliability, and says on what basis each is admitted. The classical collections gather broadly and leave assessment to the reader; this one applies the assessment first, working through the standard sources and setting aside what its criteria exclude. That inverts the usual relationship between a collection and its critical apparatus, and makes the work useful for a particular question — which reports on a subject survive a strict standard of transmission. It is best read alongside the older collections rather than instead of them: what it excludes is as much a claim as what it keeps, the criteria themselves are debated, and a report absent here may be absent because it failed a chain test rather than because the tradition doubted it. Its value is in making the grounds of inclusion explicit.
kitab-al-zuhd: An early collection by al-Ḥusayn b. Saʿīd al-Ahwāzī, a companion of the eighth, ninth and tenth Imams who settled in Qum and whose books passed into the hands of the later compilers. Its subject is renunciation: detachment from the world and a clear sight of what it is worth, restraint in appetite and speech, the remembrance of death, poverty and sufficiency, and the fear and hope the tradition treats as the proper posture toward God. The reports are short, unadorned and grouped by theme rather than argued into a case. What gives the book its particular value is its position in the chain of transmission — it belongs to the generation of primary written sources that al-Kulaynī, al-Ṣadūq and al-Ṭūsī drew upon, so it shows the raw material of the great collections before it was sorted, abridged and cross-referenced into them.
kitab-al-du-afa: Not a hadith collection but a work of rijāl — the science of assessing transmitters. It consists of entries on narrators judged weak, unreliable, or fabricators, and it is consulted when weighing whether a chain of transmission can bear the weight placed on it. Two things make it contested. Its judgements are markedly more severe than those of comparable works, condemning narrators whom al-Najāshī and al-Ṭūsī accept, which raises the question of what standard it applies. And its attribution to Aḥmad b. al-Ḥusayn Ibn al-Ghaḍāʾirī has itself been doubted, since the book reaches us through quotation in later works rather than a continuous manuscript tradition — some scholars treat it as authentic, some as compiled by another hand, some as unusable. It is therefore used with care and rarely used alone: a weakening recorded only here is generally weighed against what the other rijāl works say.
kitab-al-mu-min: Al-Ḥusayn b. Saʿīd al-Ahwāzī on the believer: the standing of a believer before God, the trials such a person is said to meet, and — the greater part of the book — the rights believers hold over one another. Visiting the sick, meeting a need before being asked, keeping a secret, feeding, clothing, withholding a harm, not turning away in anger: the narrations are concrete, mutual, and stated as obligations rather than virtues. Several make the treatment of a believer a measure of one's standing with God directly. Like the same author's Kitāb al-Zuhd it is early, short and arranged by theme, and it survives as one of the primary written sources the later compilers had in front of them, which is why passages from it recur in al-Kāfi and elsewhere in a form close to this one.
sifat-al-shi-a: A short collection by Shaykh al-Ṣadūq on what the Shīʿa are held to be — the conduct, obligations and character the narrations attach to the name. It reads as a standard rather than a description. The reports describe how such a person prays, deals in the market, speaks of others, bears difficulty and keeps trusts, and several state plainly that the name without the conduct is not the thing: that a claim of allegiance which does not show in behaviour is refused. Others distinguish those who follow the Imams in loyalty alone from those who follow them in practice. The book is brief and pointed, and is ordinarily read together with Faḍaʾil al-Shīʿa, which takes up the other side of the same subject; together they set out an expectation and a promise.
risalat-al-huquq: The Treatise on Rights, attributed to Imam ʿAlī b. al-Ḥusayn Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn (d. 95/713), and unusual in this corpus for being one continuous argument rather than a gathering of separate reports. It enumerates around fifty rights in a single sustained sequence, moving outward from the self: the right of God, then of one's own tongue, hearing, sight, hands, feet and stomach, then of the acts of worship — prayer, fasting, charity, the offering — then of those one stands in relation to: the leader, the teacher, the owner, the subject, the pupil, the spouse, the child, the parent, the sibling, and outward again to the partner, the creditor, the companion, the neighbour, the guest and the stranger. Each is stated as an obligation owed rather than a claim held, which is what gives the text its shape and its force. It is transmitted through Abū Ḥamza al-Thumālī and also preserved within al-Khiṣāl.
fada-il-al-shi-a: A brief collection by Shaykh al-Ṣadūq on the merits promised to the Shīʿa — what is said to await those who hold to the Imams, in this life and after it. The reports speak of forgiveness, intercession, the standing of their dead, and the recompense for the hardship that adherence brought in the periods when it was dangerous, which is the setting much of this material comes from. It is the companion piece to Ṣifāt al-Shīʿa: where that book sets out the conduct expected, this one sets out what is promised in return, and the two are ordinarily read and printed together. Its brevity is part of its character — it makes no argument and offers no commentary, simply gathering the reports on a single subject in one place.
